- I like R
- I like visualizing data
- I wanted to try developing a package

## My Approach

- `ggplot2` is powered by `Geom` and `Stat` objects created via the `ggproto` function
- `ggpaver` adds `GeomPavement` and `StatPavement` objects, along with `geom_pavement` and `stat_pavement` functions for use in plotting
  + The approach is similar to how `ggplot2` implements boxplots

## Just What Is a Pavement Plot Anyway?
::: {.fragment .fade-right}
```{r}
#| label: pavement-example
library(ggplot2)
library(ggpaver)
# Reset theme if necessary:
set_theme(theme())
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price, y = cut, fill = cut)) +
  geom_pavement(bins = 16, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "A pavement plot of diamond price (USD) by cut",
    subtitle = "Each tile represents an equal share of its group's data",
    caption = "Data are from `ggplot2::diamonds`"
  )
```
:::

## What Does the Code Look Like?

- Enter `ggpaver`:

::: {.fragment .fade-down}
```{.r code-line-numbers="1-10|2,5"}
library(ggplot2)
library(ggpaver)

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price, y = cut, fill = cut)) +
  geom_pavement(bins = 16, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "A Pavement Plot of Diamond Price (USD) by Cut",
    subtitle = "Each Tile Represents an Equal Share of its Group's Data",
    caption = "Data are from `ggplot2::diamonds`"
  )
```
:::

# What's Wrong with Other Plots?

## Histograms

- Groups make bins crowded
- Easy to manipulate

::: {.fragment}

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Histograms
```{r}
#| label: bad-hists
#| fig-height: 4
library(patchwork)
hist_base <- ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price, fill = cut))
p1 <- hist_base +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100) +
  labs(
    title = "Price has a right-skewed distribution",
    subtitle = "This histogram proves it"
  )
p2 <- hist_base +
  # With a simple change to bin number, the data's shape looks different:
  geom_histogram(bins = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Actually, price has a perfectly uniform distribution",
    subtitle = "This histogram proves it",
    caption = "(No it doesn't)"
  )
p1 + p2
```

### Code

```{.r code-line-numbers=2-4,9-11}
library(patchwork)
hist_base <- ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price, fill = cut))
p1 <- hist_base +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100) +
  labs(
    title = "Price has a right-skewed distribution",
    subtitle = "This histogram proves it"
  )
p2 <- hist_base +
  # With a simple change to bin number, the data's shape looks different:
  geom_histogram(bins = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Actually, price has a perfectly uniform distribution",
    subtitle = "This histogram proves it",
    caption = "(No it doesn't)"
  )
p1 + p2
```
:::
:::

## Kernal Density Estimates (KDEs)

```{r}
#| label: density
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price, color = cut, fill = cut)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4)
```
- Not necessarily intuitive to interpret
- Groups can be messy 

## Boxplots

```{r}
#| label: box
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price, y = cut, fill = cut)) +
  geom_boxplot(
    quantile.type = 2,
    width = 0.5,
    alpha = 0.75,
    show.legend = FALSE
  )
```
- Better than the aforementioned alternatives, but ...
- Depending on the viewer's background, it may not be obvious what the box, whiskers, and outliers each represent
- Not ideal for multimodal data—there's a reason that they're called *boxplots* instead of ***boxes****-plots*

## Example: Bimodal Data

```{r}
#| label: change-theme
set_theme(
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank()
  )
)
```
::: {.panel-tabset}

### Boxplot
```{r}
#| label: bimodal-boxplot
set.seed(20261015)
n <- 10000
x1 <- rnorm(n, mean = 250, sd = 50)
x2 <- rnorm(n, mean = 750, sd = 100)
bimodal <- data.frame(x = c(x1, x2))
# Saving title string since I'll be using it again:
bimodal_title <- "The presented variable's distribution is bimodal"

ggplot(bimodal, aes(x = x)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = bimodal_title,
    subtitle = "You wouldn't know it from looking at this plot"
  )
```

### Code
```{r}
#| label: bimodal-boxplot-display
#| ref.label: bimodal-boxplot
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
```

:::

## Pavement to the Rescue!
::: {.panel-tabset}

### Pavement Plot
```{r}
#| label: pavement-boxplot
pavement <- ggplot(bimodal, aes(x = x)) +
  geom_pavement(bins = 16) +
  labs(x = NULL)
box <- ggplot(bimodal, aes(x = x)) + geom_boxplot()

patchwork1 <- pavement / box
patchwork1 +
  plot_annotation(
    title = bimodal_title,
    subtitle = "You WOULD know it from looking at this plot, thanks to ggpaver",
    caption = "Boxplot included for comparison"
  )
```

### Code 
```{r}
#| label: pavement-boxplot-display
#| ref.label: pavement-boxplot
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
```

:::

## What about Violin Plots?
::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| label: violin-quantile
n_bins <- 16
# From `stat_pavement()`:
quantiles <- seq(0, 1, length.out = n_bins + 1)
ggplot(bimodal, aes(x = x, y = 1)) +
  geom_violin(
    quantiles = quantiles,
    quantile.linetype = 1
  ) +
  labs(
    title = bimodal_title,
    subtitle = "You can tell from this violin plot",
    caption = "It even has quantile lines added",
    y = NULL
  )
```
:::

## Well...

- They trade the boxplot's simplicity for flexibility—a good trade, but still a trade
- Pavement plots are *both simple **and** flexible*

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| label: plots-compared
violin <- ggplot(bimodal, aes(x = x, y = 1)) +
  geom_violin(
    quantiles = quantiles,
    quantile.linetype = 1
  ) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
box <- ggplot(bimodal, aes(x = x)) + geom_boxplot() + labs(x = NULL)
pavement <- ggplot(bimodal, aes(x = x)) +
  geom_pavement(bins = 16)
# Patch together:
patchwork2 <- violin / box / pavement
# Add annotation for entire patchwork rather than constituent plots:
patchwork2 +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "One Distribution, Three Visualizations",
    subtitle = "Take your pick",
    caption = "(Pick pavement)"
  )
```
:::

- Extend functionality

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| label: ggMarginal-example
library(ggplot2)
library(ggExtra)

scatter <- ggplot(
  penguins,
  aes(x = bill_dep, y = flipper_len, color = species)
) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Imagine this (from `ggExtra::ggMarginal`) but with pavement instead of boxplots",
    caption = "Data are from `datasets::penguins`"
  )
# `ggMarginal` adds univariate plots to the margins of a main multivariate one.
ggMarginal(scatter, type = "boxplot", groupColour = TRUE, groupFill = TRUE)
```
:::
